video.title: How good is my model?: Accuracy, mistakes and thresholds
video.format_note: Animated explainer, 16:9, flat Darsi colours on paper-grey backgrounds. Charts draw themselves; code is typed out on a card, left to right in both languages. Narration in the lesson language; captions as separate files, never burned in.
cast: Ms Amina Bello - primary teacher, Nigeria (main character)
Narrator - the Darsi voice (warm, peer to peer)

scenes.narration: Our school tried a model to warn us early about pupils who might need extra help. It was ninety percent accurate. Then we noticed it had not warned us about a single pupil.
Today: how to judge a model by the mistakes it makes.

scenes.on_screen_text: Accuracy: the share it gets right
scenes.narration: Accuracy is the share of cases the model gets right. But if only one pupil in ten needs help, a model that always says no help is already ninety percent accurate. Accuracy alone can hide a useless model.
A model can make two kinds of mistake. A false alarm warns about a pupil who is fine. A miss stays quiet about a pupil who really needs help, and at school a miss usually costs more.
We count all four results for one hundred pupils. Eight were caught, two were missed, six were false alarms and eighty four were rightly left alone.
Many models give each pupil a score from zero to one. We choose a threshold, and pupils above it get a warning. Lower the threshold and you catch more pupils, but you also raise more false alarms.

Choosing the threshold is not a maths question. A false alarm costs a short chat with a teacher, while a miss can cost a pupil a year. So we chose a low threshold, and a teacher always checks each warning.
Quick check! One pupil in ten needs help, and a model always says no help. It is ninety percent accurate. Is it a good model?
No. It misses every single pupil who needs help. Always look at the misses and the false alarms, not only the accuracy.
In the app, open the threshold lab. Slide the threshold down and up, and watch the four boxes of the confusion matrix change.
Your turn. What happens when we lower the threshold for a warning?
We catch more pupils, and we get more false alarms. Remember: accuracy can hide misses, count both kinds of mistake, and let people choose the threshold.

Try it in class tomorrow: draw a two by two table on the board and fill it with a made-up rain forecast for twenty days. Ask pupils which mistake is worse: an umbrella you didn't need, or getting soaked?
